key_insight: The intact brain–skull interface is better represented by a cohesive zone model than by rigid attachment or frictionless sliding, with failure occurring within the subarachnoid space.
engineering_relevance: Experimentally calibrated interface properties can improve boundary and contact conditions in computational head models.
method: Test native brain–skull specimens from 19 sheep cadaver heads under tension, compression and shear.
Use MRI-derived geometry to build specimen-specific finite element models.
Apply inverse finite element analysis to calibrate Ogden brain tissue parameters, then cohesive interface parameters.
evidence_signal: Brain shear modulus increased from 0.94 to 1.60 kPa across tested strain rates, while interface properties showed no significant rate or loading-mode dependence: peak normal traction 2.35 ± 0.81 kPa, peak tangential traction 4.14 ± 0.97 kPa and fracture energy 0.35 ± 0.14 N/m.
watch_item: Parameters derived from sheep cadaver specimens require validation before use in human head models or extrapolation beyond the tested loading rates.
paper_title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
